metric_rationale: This metric isolates the specific trials in the design where Tallying and WADD make diametrically opposite predictions. On trials where one option has 3 less-valid features and the other has 2 highly-valid features, Tallying strictly prefers the option with 3 features (ignoring validity), while WADD prefers the option with 2 features (because their combined validity outweighs the 3). By calculating the proportion of choices that align with Tallying on these specific trials, we expect a value significantly above 0.5 for Tallying and significantly below 0.5 for WADD, cleanly discriminating the two models.

Focuses on the two trials where WADD and Tallying have completely opposing, deterministic preferences. In Trial 1, WADD strongly prefers B (response 1) because of the two highest-validity features, while Tallying prefers A (response 0) due to a higher quantity of lower-validity features. In Trial 4, the options are swapped, so WADD prefers A (response 0) and Tallying prefers B (response 1). The difference in mean response between Trial 1 and Trial 4 will be strongly positive for WADD (~1.0) and strongly negative for Tallying (~-1.0).

This metric calculates the proportion of times the subject chooses option B on trials where option B has a strictly greater number of positive features than option A. Take The Best (TTB) will consistently choose option A on these trials because option A was designed to always possess the single highest-validity discriminating cue. In contrast, the Weighted Additive (WADD) model is compensatory; it will frequently choose option B because the combined weight of option B's numerous lower-validity cues typically outweighs option A's single high-validity cue. This creates a maximal behavioral divergence between the two models.

This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice matches the prediction of the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic. TTB compares features in descending order of validity and stops at the first discriminating feature. In this specific experimental design, the WADD model and TTB make opposite predictions on 4 out of the 6 trial types because the WADD model allows multiple lower-validity features to compensate for the highest-validity feature. Thus, data generated by TTB will yield a high match rate (close to 1.0, minus lapse noise), whereas data generated by WADD will yield a consistently low match rate (close to 0.33, as it only agrees with TTB on 2 out of 6 trial types). This creates a massive, stable gap between the two theories.

The pure Take The Best (TTB) model ignores all features except the first one that discriminates between the options. In this experimental design, the highest validity discriminating feature always favors Option A. Thus, TTB predicts a constant probability of choosing A across all trials, leading to a correlation of 0 between the WADD score difference (A - B) and the choice of A. In contrast, the Strategy Selection (TTB + WADD) model incorporates the WADD heuristic, meaning the probability of choosing A will increase as the compensatory support for Option B decreases. This results in a strongly positive correlation between the WADD score difference and the probability of choosing A.

The experimental design consists of trials where the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic invariably favors Option A. However, the compensatory support (captured by the Weighted Additive or WADD score) systematically varies across these trials. By calculating the difference in the probability of choosing Option A between trials where WADD also favors Option A and trials where WADD favors Option B, we can cleanly separate the two theories. Pure TTB predicts this difference should be zero (since TTB always points to A), whereas the Strategy Selection Theory (TTB + WADD) predicts a positive difference because the WADD component pulls choices toward B in the latter subset of trials.

By comparing the subject's adherence to the Take-The-Best (TTB) prediction on trials where the downstream tally agrees with TTB versus trials where it disagrees, we can isolate the effect of the downstream tally. Under the pure TTB model, adherence should be equal across both types of trials (difference near zero). Under the Downstream Tallying Mixture model, adherence will be significantly higher when the tally agrees and significantly lower when it disagrees, yielding a positive difference.

This metric isolates trials where the discriminating cue consistently favors Option A, but the downstream tally of unexamined cues systematically varies. In the 'high_tally_A' trials, the remaining cues strongly favor Option A, whereas in 'high_tally_B' trials, the remaining cues strongly favor Option B. The pure Take The Best (TTB) model ignores these downstream cues and predicts a constant probability of choosing A across both sets of trials, resulting in a metric value near 0. The TTB + Downstream Tallying Mixture model, however, adjusts its choice probabilities based on the tally of unexamined cues, predicting a higher rate of choosing A in the first set and a lower rate in the second, leading to a significantly positive metric value.
